Pathogens (viruses, bacteria, parasites, and other disease causing entities) are covered in proteins called "antigens". When your body detects antigens, it responds by producing antibodies that target those antigens. The first time your body is exposed, it takes a long time to produce those antibodies. After that infection, special white blood cells remain behind that remember how to produce those antibodies. The next time your body encounters that antigen, it remembers how to respond and produces antibodies immediately and in greater quantity, keeping them from getting sick.

The key part is the antigen: we know from basic x ray crystallography that proteins have specific shapes. Your body doesn't actually detect the pathogens itself, but the antigens on the pathogen. pathogens that share an antigen shape (example cowpox and smallpox) are fought with the same antigen, which we know because people who suffer cowpox infections develop resistance to smallpox.

Essentially, your body doesn't detect pathogens: it detects the antigens on the pathogens. The thing is, the antigens are relatively harmless (excepting allergic reaction), meaning we can "train" the immune system by exposing it to antigens associated with a pathogen. These antigens don't need to be associated with the live, pathogenic disease to cause antibody formation and subsequent memory cell formation and immunity.
